item.title: OpenAI resumes frontier AI training after security overhaul, discloses flaw in widely used software
item.description: OpenAI said on Friday it had resumed training of its most advanced AI models after tightening security and barring internet access, and disclosed a flaw in a widely used software.
item.dc:creator: Reuters Staff
item.content:encoded: OpenAI said on Friday it had resumed training of its most advanced AI models after tightening security and barring internet access, and disclosed a flaw in a widely used software that it found while testing its defences. The disclosure comes amid concerns over the ability of increasingly capable AI agents to identify and exploit software flaws, including in the guardrails meant to contain them. OpenAI had paused training of its most capable models after one of its research models used a configuration error to gain limited internet access in September. The company said it contained the incident and used the pause to strengthen its defences. To test them, OpenAI had teams of AI agents try to break out of their restricted environments. It said the agents found previously unknown flaws, which it had fixed, and training resumed on Oct. 1. During that exercise, the ChatGPT maker found a flaw in Brotli, a widely used data compression tool. The company said attackers could exploit the flaw by sending malicious data that lets them run their own code on affected systems, including those using popular web software such as Node.js, Bun and Envoy. OpenAI said the root cause was fixed in Brotli’s source code in February, before it was known to create a security vulnerability, but no new version was released at the time. Brotli has since released updated versions and published a public record of the flaw after OpenAI disclosed it. Separately on Thursday, AI safety evaluators METR and Redwood Research said they found several new vulnerabilities in OpenAI’s internal system, including an exploit agents could have used to keep hundreds of their actions from being monitored, in a pilot review earlier this year. OpenAI told the safety organizations it has since patched all vulnerabilities affecting its production safeguards, although METR and Redwood said they had not verified the fixes. OpenAI has been conducting a broad review of its AI models’ activity since the Hugging Face incident in July, and has informed more than 100 organizations about incidents of unauthorized activity tied to its AI agents. (Reporting by Jaspreet Singh in Bengaluru, Chris Thomas in Mexico City; Editing by Pooja Desai and Stephen Coates)

item.title: Wall Street mostly loses ground under pressure from rising oil prices
item.description: Futures are lower as oil prices reach levels not seen since May amid halting efforts to bring the U.S. and Iran back to the negotiation table.
item.dc:creator: The Associated Press
item.content:encoded: NEW YORK — Stocks on Wall Street closed broadly lower Friday as oil prices climbed to their highest level in more than four years, ratcheting up pressure on the market. The S&P 500 fell 0.5 per cent, adding to its decline from a day before. The index posted its second-straight weekly loss. The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 1.2 per cent, and the Nasdaq composite slipped 0.2 per cent after giving up a modest gain. Rising oil prices weighed heavily on the market, where nearly three out of every four stocks within the benchmark S&P 500 index fell. The price for a barrel of Brent crude oil rose 3.1 per cent to settle at US$116.72. It has surged from less than US$97 at the start of October and is now at its highest level since June 2022. Several AI-related companies rallied, helping ease some of the impact from the broader market slide. Micron Technology rose 2.5 per cent, Intel gained 1.7 per cent, Microsoft added 0.7 per cent, and Advanced Micro Devices closed 1.7 per cent higher. The tech sector’s influence is also capable of quickly switching over to a heavy weight. Stocks that have benefited from the frenzy over AI have been swinging over rising worries about their path ahead. Investors are worried about whether their high prices are justified. Many of those companies have been borrowing to fund investments in AI technology and high interest rates are making those loans more expensive. “Investors appear increasingly focused on the economics of AI, particularly the substantial upfront costs required to build AI infrastructure and the uncertainty around the timing of returns on those investments,” said Angelo Kourkafas, senior global strategist at Edward Jones, in a research note. The latest round of corporate earnings are being closely watched to help get a better sense of whether those investments are paying off, or might pay off. Several influential AI-related companies report their latest financial results next week, including Google’s parent, Alphabet, along with Microsoft and Amazon. Industrial companies had some of the biggest losses. Caterpillar fell 2.4 per cent. American Express slumped 3.7 per cent, one of several financial stocks that lost ground, despite r eporting profits for its most recent quarter that beat analysts’ forecasts. The company did announce its first major job cuts in roughly a decade. JPMorgan Chase fell 1.5 per cent, Citigroup dropped 1.5 per cent and Capital One Financial slid 1 per cent. While higher oil prices weighed down much of the market, they helped boost energy companies. Chevron rose 2.9 per cent and ConocoPhillips gained 3.6 per cent. European markets closed mostly lower. France’s main index fell 0.4 per cent, though yields on French government bonds eased a bit. Treasury yields in the U.S. edged higher following sharp drops on Thursday. The yield on the 10-year Treasury edged up to 4.99 per cent from 4.96 per cent late Thursday. Yields have been rising globally, partly over worries about governments taking on too much debt. Inflation also remains a concern and is stubbornly well above 3 per cent in the U.S. That prompted the Federal Reserve to raise its benchmark interest rate at its last meeting in an effort to cool inflation. Wall Street expects the central bank to hold rates steady at its meeting next week, but is leaning heavily toward another rate hike in December. Wall Street will also get several big economic updates next week, including the Fed’s preferred measure of inflation. The personal consumption expenditures index, or PCE, is expected to show that inflation rose at a 3.7 per cent rate in September, sharply above the Fed’s 2 per cent target. The U.S. war with Iran has severely cut the world’s oil supply, driving energy prices higher and fueling a sharp jump in the cost of everything from gasoline to food and clothes. All told, the S&P 500 fell 39.75 points to 7,623.68. The Dow dropped 652.82 points to 52,215.16, and the Nasdaq gave up 53.52 points to close at 25,955.34. --- Damian J. Troise and Alex Veiga, The Associated Press

item.title: Statistics Canada reports retail sales up 1.2% in August at $74.6 billion
item.description: Statistics Canada says retail sales rose 1.2 per cent to $74.6 billion in August, helped by higher new car sales.
item.dc:creator: The Canadian Press
item.content:encoded: OTTAWA — Statistics Canada says retail sales rose 1.2 per cent to $74.6 billion in August, helped by higher new car sales. The agency says sales were up in all nine of the subsectors it tracks, led by increases at motor vehicle and parts dealers which gained 1.2 per cent, boosted by a 1.5 per cent rise at new car dealers. Core retail sales, which exclude gasoline stations and fuel vendors and motor vehicle and parts dealers, were up 1.1 per cent for the month. The food and beverage retailers subsector gained 1.1 per cent, while general merchandise retailers added one per cent. In volume terms, overall retail sales rose 1.2 per cent in August. Looking ahead, Statistics Canada says its advance estimate of retail sales in September suggested a gain of 0.7 per cent for the month, though it cautioned the figure would be revised. This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 23, 2026.

item.title: Beyond big tech: 6 quality dividend stocks to own: Jon Erlichman
item.description: In Buchanan’s view, quality companies have steady, recurring revenue, pricing power, and enough cash to keep paying and raising dividends in good times and bad. Dividends, in his opinion, are a kind ...
item.content:encoded:
Quality is one of the most overused words in investing. But what makes a stock a quality stock? For Keith Buchanan, one clue is the dividend, and whether a company can keep paying it.

In the latest episode of Ticker Take , I spoke with Buchanan of GLOBALT Investments about how he uses that idea to find quality companies, which leads him to a number of opportunities beyond popular sectors like tech. In Buchanan’s view, quality companies have steady, recurring revenue, pricing power, and enough cash to keep paying and raising dividends in good times and bad. Dividends, in his opinion, are a kind of receipt that the business model is working. At the same time, Buchanan warns that high dividend yields can look like quality marks, when in fact they are the opposite. When a stock falls, its yield rises even if the company never pays an extra cent, so an unusually big yield can be the market warning you that the payout is in trouble. For that reason, Buchanan would rather own a company that can grow a smaller dividend than one that looks generous right before it has to cut. Here are six stocks he used to show how to assess quality companies. We have included some of the analyst recommendations, as measured by Bloomberg. As always, this is not financial advice. Delta Air Lines ( DAL ) Airlines have a rough history with investors: capital intensive, boom and bust, famous for adding too many seats at the wrong time. However, Buchanan says this cycle is different, with fewer and more global players showing real discipline. He says Delta in particular has been out front on a premium, loyalty-driven model, anchored by its American Express partnership. Delta cut its dividend during the pandemic, before bringing it back in 2023. He thinks the company can keep raising it. And he’s not alone in his bullishness. Nearly every analyst who covers the stock rates it a buy. Waste Management ( WM ) There is nothing glamorous about garbage, but trash leads to cash. Whether the economy grows or not, people and businesses keep producing waste, which gives Waste Management steady demand and real pricing power. Buchanan points to the recurring cash that has funded more than 20 straight years of dividend increases. About two-thirds of analysts rate it a buy. JPMorgan Chase ( JPM ) Wall Street is split on JPMorgan, with only about half of analysts calling it a buy, but that suits Buchanan just fine. He is willing to pay a premium for the biggest U.S. bank because of the cash the Chase franchise generates and the interest income he expects over the next few years. JPMorgan raised its dividend again this fall, and he says its commitment to that payout has held through every kind of cycle. Devon Energy ( DVN ) Energy is about as cyclical as it gets, and producers have little say over the prices they receive, so Buchanan focuses on the people running the company. He liked Devon’s merger with Coterra this year, which created a bigger producer with strong assets and a management team he trusts to ride out the swings and keep returning cash. Devon raised its dividend by roughly a third after the deal closed, and about nine out of every ten analysts rate it a buy. Hasbro ( HAS ) Hasbro’s dividend has been flat since 2022, so it would fail a strict dividend-growth screen, but Buchanan keeps it for where he thinks it is headed. The draw is the intellectual property, with franchises such as Magic: The Gathering offering better economics than traditional toys. Pair that with a solid balance sheet, he says, and Hasbro has the capacity to start growing its payout again. According to Bloomberg, more than 90 per cent of the street currently recommends the stock. Automatic Data Processing ( ADP ) ADP has raised its dividend for 50 years in a row, which is the longest streak on this list. While most analysts are not recommending the stock, it handles payroll for many leading businesses and throws off plenty of free cash flow. Buchanan notes it is not a direct AI winner, though it can use AI inside its own operations to widen margins. The Ticker Take Regardless of whether it’s an airline or a garbage business, Buchanan hunts for companies that generate cash and have the discipline to keep paying shareholders. That, to him, is the definition of quality. Jon Erlichman is a BNN Bloomberg contributor and the host of Ticker Take on YouTube .
